d.title: Three models, three answers to where the modalities meet
d.caption: The first column is the design decision and everything else follows from it. **CLIP's towers never meet — no cross-attention at all — which is what makes it a retrieval model rather than a reasoning one.** LLaVA projects ViT patches **into the LLM's token stream**, so vision becomes text as far as the model is concerned. **Flamingo inserts gated cross-attention between frozen towers, so only the inserted layers train** — which is why it is the few-shot one: the language model is untouched.

d.title: The ordering is exactly right and every value is above 0.73
d.caption: **dog/puppy 0.959 > dog/cat 0.931 > dog/car 0.878 > dog/city 0.735** — the ranking is correct at every step. And the absolute values are all high and compressed into a narrow band, **which is the same anisotropy 3.6 found in BERT's final layer: read the gap, not the raw cosine.** The learned temperature explains how a 0.07 gap becomes a decision: **`logit_scale = 4.6052`, so `exp(4.6052) = 100.00`, and every similarity is multiplied by a hundred before the softmax.**

d.title: A 1024-pixel image does not fit in a 4k context at all
d.caption: **256 visual tokens at 224×224 is 6.2% of a 4k context; 5,329 tokens at 1024×1024 is 130.1% — the image alone overflows the window before any text.** Which is the constraint that shapes every vision-language design: **resolution is context budget**, so Flamingo's Perceiver Resampler compressing to a fixed 64 tokens is not a refinement but the thing that makes multi-image conversation possible at all.

d.title: The gate starts at zero, so training begins from exactly the original model
d.caption: **Each inserted cross-attention layer starts with a `tanh` gate initialised at zero, so at the start of training the model is *exactly* the original LM** — visual influence is learned gradually rather than imposed. Both towers stay frozen, **so the LM's language ability cannot be degraded by multimodal training, which is a real risk in the LLaVA approach.** The cost is honest: **cross-attention layers are real added compute in every forward pass, unlike LLaVA's projection, which is paid once per image.**

nodes.label: Gated: tanh initialised at zero
nodes.sub: training starts AT the original LM

d.title: Nothing in modules 4 and 5 stops applying
d.caption: **Visual tokens go through the same attention, the same KV cache and the same quantisation** — so there is no separate multimodal performance story to learn. 4.3's `O(n²)` is **what makes high resolution expensive**, which is §04 restated. And 5.2's cache arithmetic **now includes hundreds of visual tokens per image, which is why a multi-image conversation exhausts memory far faster than a text one of the same apparent length.**

nodes.label: Same attention (4.3)
nodes.sub: so O(n^2) in visual tokens too

nodes.label: Which is why resolution is expensive

d.title: Sixty-four times the parameters at twice the compute
d.caption: **Total parameters grow with the expert count; compute per token does not — it is fixed by `top_k`.** So 128 experts at top-2 is **64× the parameters of a dense FFN at 2.0× its compute**, and the compute column is constant from 2 experts onward. The deployed ratios are lower than the table's ceiling because attention is not replicated: **Mixtral 8x7B is 46.7B total and 12.9B active (3.6×), DeepSeek-V3 is 671B and 37B (18.1×).**

d.title: Routing is per token, and the layer is shape-preserving
d.caption: **The first token goes to experts [4, 6] with weights [0.6088, 0.3912], summing to exactly 1.0** — and routing is **per token, not per sequence**, so different words in the same sentence go to different experts and the same word can route differently depending on context. The layer is shape-preserving — **(2, 10, 64) in and out — so it drops into a transformer block exactly where the FFN was**, which is why MoE is a substitution rather than a redesign.

d.title: A 0.5 logit head start became 46% of all tokens, and stayed there
d.caption: Top-1 routing over 8 experts with one expert given a 0.5 head start — **standing in for the random initial asymmetry any real model has.** Without a load-balancing loss it **never recovers: 42.6% at step 0, 46.3% at step 599**, with final entropy 1.7098 against a uniform 2.0794. With the auxiliary loss at `α = 0.05` the same run **falls to 15.0% busiest and entropy 2.0720 — essentially uniform.** And the MSE is unchanged (0.0316 against 0.0321), **so balance cost nothing in task loss here.**

d.title: One term carries no gradient and the other carries all of it
d.caption: **`f_i` is the fraction of tokens routed to expert `i` — discrete, computed by counting, and it carries no gradient. `P_i` is the mean router probability — continuous, and where all the gradient flows.** Their product is minimised when both are uniform, and the arithmetic is clean: **at `f_i = P_i = 1/N` the sum is exactly 1.0 for any `N`, and total collapse onto one expert gives `N`.** `α` is typically **0.01** — **a nudge that prevents collapse, not an objective that overrides the task.**

d.title: Sixty gigabytes resident to use fifteen
d.caption: **All 60.1 GB of experts must be resident, because the router picks per token and you cannot know in advance which experts a sequence will need — while the active compute is 15.0 GB worth of weights.** Which is exactly why MoE is cheap to *train* and awkward to *serve*: **you pay dense memory for sparse compute**, and the memory is what a serving deployment is constrained by. One expert in one layer is only 0.23 GB — **the problem is the product of 8 and 32.**

d.title: A continuous dynamical system, discretised into a recurrence
d.caption: **`h'(t) = A h(t) + B x(t)` is a latent state evolving under an input — control theory, not sequence modelling.** Discretise it by zero-order hold or a bilinear transform and **you get `h_k = Ā h_{k−1} + B̄ x_k`, a recurrence over sequence positions.** Which is the whole move: **the model is specified in continuous time and run in discrete steps, so the step size `Δ` becomes a parameter** — and Mamba's selectivity in §05 is exactly making that parameter depend on the input.

nodes.label: And delta is what Mamba makes learnable

d.title: The recurrence and the convolution agree to 4.77e-07
d.caption: **Because the recurrence is linear it unrolls in closed form, so `y_k` is a convolution with a kernel `K_j = C Āⱼ B̄` computable in advance** — which is the duality that makes SSMs trainable: **run it as a convolution in parallel for training, and as a recurrence one step at a time for inference.** Verified: identical outputs to within float noise. And the kernel decays — **`|A| < 1` means `Aⱼ` shrinks with `j`, so distant inputs contribute less, and the rate of that decay *is* the memory horizon.**

d.title: The half-life is the memory, and it is brutally sensitive to A
d.caption: **At `A = 0.5` the half-life is 1.0 step and `|A|^50` is 8.9e−16 — the state has forgotten everything. At `A = 0.999` the half-life is 692.8 steps.** So **a hand-initialised `A` has to be accurate to three decimal places to give a useful memory horizon**, which is precisely the problem HiPPO solves: it derives an initialisation for `A` that provably approximates the whole input history, rather than leaving the memory length to chance.

d.title: 4.2 MB at any length, against 524 GB at a million tokens
d.caption: **The SSM state is 4.2 MB regardless of sequence length — that is the structural claim, and it is what an RNN always had.** The comparison is the reason anyone cares: **a transformer's KV cache is 1.07 GB at 2,048 tokens (256× the state) and 524.29 GB at a million (125,000×).** Which is also the honest cost: **a fixed-size state cannot hold everything, so the trade is bounded memory against lossy recall** — and 4.1's capacity argument now runs the other way.

d.title: Delta varies tenfold across the input, which is the selectivity
d.caption: **S4's `A`, `B` and `C` are fixed, so the same filter is applied to every input regardless of content — the model cannot decide that *this* token matters more than that one.** Mamba makes them functions of the input, and the measurement shows the effect: **`Δ` ranges over [0.0198, 0.2189], an 11× spread, which produces `Ā` values from 0.9804 to 0.8034.** Read as half-lives that is **a memory horizon that varies per token** — content-dependent forgetting, which is what attention had and S4 did not.

state: the same filter for every input
what attention had, S4 did not

d.title: Half a terabyte of KV cache for one million tokens
d.caption: A 32-layer, 4096-wide 7B model at a million tokens in fp16: **524.3 GB with full multi-head attention, 131.1 GB with GQA8.** Neither fits on any single accelerator, **and the weights are 14 GB** — so at this length **the model is a rounding error and the cache is the system.** Which frames everything that follows: the techniques in this lesson are about the cache and the score matrix, not about the parameters.

d.title: Four devices, four partial answers, and the last one is exact
d.caption: **Each device attends to one KV block at a time and must combine `P` partial results into the true softmax over all `N` keys — which is precisely 5.2's running-statistics update, so FlashAttention's online softmax is the enabling idea for ring attention rather than merely a related one.** The partials are meaningless on the way: **+0.334320, then +0.137551, then +0.122937** — and the final value is **+0.187467 against full attention's +0.187466, a difference of 7.45e-08.**

d.title: A 4,096-token window reaches 131,072 tokens once you stack 32 layers
d.caption: **Restricting every token to the previous `W` positions is `O(N·W)` instead of `O(N²)`, and it looks like it should destroy long-range dependency — except that stacking layers recovers it.** Each layer extends the reach by `W`, so **Mistral 7B's 32 layers × 4096 is 131,072 tokens of effective reach.** And the saving grows with length: **2× less compute at 8,192 tokens, 8× at 32,768, 32× at 131,072** — because the window is constant while full attention is not.

d.title: Six ways to extend a trained model, and two of them need no fine-tuning
d.caption: The first three are all operations on RoPE's frequency spectrum from 4.9. **Position Interpolation scales the indices and compresses high-frequency detail uniformly; NTK-aware raises the base so high frequencies are barely touched and low ones stretch, and often works with no fine-tuning at all; YaRN adds attention temperature and took LLaMA-3 from 8K to 128K.** The last two change the architecture instead: **landmark tokens summarise preceding context, and Infini-attention keeps a fixed-size compressive memory.**

items.label: NTK-aware scaling
items.sub: raise the RoPE base; low frequencies stretch

items.label: Dynamic NTK
items.sub: scale by the actual length, at inference

d.title: The U-shape is two mechanisms this course already measured
d.caption: Needle-in-a-haystack accuracy is **high at the start, high at the end, with a pronounced dip in the middle** — and both halves have a measured cause. **Attention sinks: 4.4 measured a head sending 86.4% of its mass to a structural token, and early positions attract attention regardless of content. RoPE's decay: 4.9 measured aligned scores falling to 5.36% of their distance-0 value by 2,048 positions.** **The beginning is favoured by the first, the end by the second, and the middle gets neither** — so **measure effective context rather than reading it off a spec sheet.**

nodes.label: So 128K may degrade past 32K
nodes.sub: measure, do not read the spec

d.title: Four parallelisms, and each one is named for what it cannot do
d.caption: Read the cost column as the selection rule. **Data parallel is the cheapest and requires the full model on every device, so it solves nothing about model size.** Tensor parallel splits individual matrices and pays **high communication per layer.** Pipeline parallel splits layers and pays **bubble overhead between stages.** And sequence/ring parallel is the only one that addresses context length — **at the price of a high-bandwidth ring topology**, which is why it is a datacentre technique rather than a general one.
